transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, hi, Doctor. I'm... I'm here because my manager at the restaurant told me I had to come see someone if I wanted to keep my shifts. I've been a waitress there for three years, you know? And I'm usually really good, like, I can balance four plates on one arm and I never forget a side of ranch. But lately, things have just been... getting tangled up. What really scared everyone at work, and I guess what scared me too, is that I started just... freezing up in the middle of service. Like, right in the middle of the dinner rush. Or I'd start doing things completely out of order. The other night, I was just standing by the soda station for I don't even know how long, holding the key to the cash drawer, and I was just repeating table numbers out loud. "Table four, table twelve, table nine." Over and over. I was supposed to be closing out checks, but I just stood there with the key, staring at the ice machine, saying the numbers. My manager had to come tap me on the shoulder and ask me what I was doing, and I couldn't even really explain it to him because it felt like the numbers were the only thing that made sense right then. So he told me I couldn't come back until I got a doctor's note saying I was okay to work.
When those episodes happen, do you later have a gap in your memory for what you did or said during them?

No, I don't think so. I mean, it's not like a blackout or anything like that. I remember standing there. I remember the cold air coming off the ice machine, and I remember the exact feeling of the metal key pressing into the palm of my hand. It had a little jagged edge on one side that I kept running my thumb over. And I remember hearing myself say the numbers. "Table four, table twelve, table nine." It wasn't like I was asleep or unconscious. I was completely awake. But it's more like... my brain just gets stuck on a loop, you know? Like a record skipping, if people even know what that means anymore. I used to have this old record player in my dorm room when I was taking classes at the community college—just a few semesters, business admin, though I never finished—and it would hit a scratch and just play the same three seconds of a song over and over until you physically moved the needle. That's what it feels like. I'm there, I'm aware of my surroundings, I can see the wait station and hear the kitchen printer going off, but I just can't move the needle myself. I just have to keep doing the thing I'm doing until someone else, like my manager, comes along and kind of bumps the record player for me. So, no, the memory is all there, it's just... the control isn't, I guess? Or the ability to do the next step just vanishes.
Do these episodes usually happen when you’re under a lot of stress?

I mean... I don't really know if stress is the trigger. You'd think so, right? Because a dinner rush is stressful. It's loud, the kitchen gets backed up, people are waving you down for refills, and the ticket machine is just printing and printing. But the thing is, I've worked in restaurants since I was nineteen. I actually used to thrive on that energy. I used to love the chaos of a Friday night when every table is full and you're just flying through the dining room. It felt like a dance. So the stress... it's not new stress, you know? And it doesn't only happen when it's crazy busy. Like, last Tuesday, it was a totally dead afternoon shift. Maybe three tables in the whole place. I was rolling silverware in the back, which is usually the most relaxing part of the day, just folding the napkins, tucking in the forks and knives, making these neat little bundles. It's so repetitive and quiet. And I was just standing there, and suddenly I couldn't stop folding this one napkin. I just kept smoothing it out, folding it in half, unfolding it, smoothing it out again. Over and over. There was no rush, no one yelling for me, no stress at all. Just me and this black cloth napkin. I must have stood there doing it for twenty minutes before the bartender walked back and asked if I was okay. So... I guess I'm not really sure if stress has anything to do with it, because it seems to happen whether I'm carrying a tray of hot food through a crowd or just standing in an empty room doing side work. It's just so unpredictable, which honestly is what stresses me out the most now. The not knowing when the record is going to skip again.
During these episodes, do you ever feel like you are choosing or acting them out on purpose?

No, no, definitely not on purpose. I mean, why would I? It's embarrassing. It's so embarrassing. Like with the napkin thing I just mentioned, folding and unfolding it... if I was doing that on purpose, I would have stopped the second I realized how ridiculous it looked. But I couldn't. It's like... it's like my hands were doing it, and my brain was watching my hands do it, but there was no connection between the two. There's no part of me that thinks, "Oh, I'm going to stand by the soda machine and say table numbers now." I don't want to do these things. I want to be working. I need my job. I have rent, I have my car payment—it's a 2014 Civic, and it's mostly reliable, but it needs new brake pads soon, and I can't afford that if I'm not picking up shifts. So, no, I'm not choosing this. It feels like the opposite of choosing. It feels like the choice is completely taken away from me. I'm just sort of trapped inside the action while it's happening, waiting for it to be over, waiting for someone to snap me out of it so I can just go back to being normal and doing my job. I'd give anything to just be able to choose to stop when it happens.
Have you ever had a seizure?

A seizure? Like, falling down and shaking? No, I've never had anything like that. I mean, my aunt on my mom's side had epilepsy, I think? Or maybe it was my great-aunt. I remember my mom talking about it when I was really little, how they had to be careful with flashing lights and stuff. But I've never had anything like that happen to me. I've never passed out or convulsed or bitten my tongue. And like I was saying before, I'm completely awake when these weird stuck moments happen. My eyes are open, I'm standing up, I'm not falling over or losing my balance. I'm just... frozen in whatever I'm doing. So it doesn't feel like a medical emergency in that way, you know? It's not like my body is spasming. It's just my actions that get stuck. I've never even fainted in my life, honestly. Not even when I had to get my blood drawn for a physical a few years ago, and I hate needles. I get super lightheaded, but I always stay conscious. So, no, definitely no seizures. Unless... I mean, unless there's a type of seizure where you just stand there and repeat things? But even then, I feel like a doctor would have caught that when I was younger. I was a pretty healthy kid, mostly just ear infections and stuff. So, yeah, no seizures that I know of.
When these episodes happen, do you find yourself making the same repetitive movements over and over, like folding, tapping, or repeating actions in a fixed pattern?

Well, yes, I mean, like I was saying with the napkin, right? Folding and unfolding it. That's definitely one of them. But it's not just the folding. It's... it's the whole pattern of how I get stuck, and it's really starting to freak people out at work. What really scared everyone, and honestly scared me too, is that I started freezing up right in the middle of service. Like, right in the thick of it. I'll be in the middle of doing something completely normal, and then I just... derail. Like, the other day, I was supposed to be closing out checks. We have this old point-of-sale system, it's super clunky, you have to use a physical key to pop the cash drawer if you're settling a cash payment. So I had the cash drawer key in my hand, and I was standing by the soda station, which isn't even where the terminal is. The terminal is on the other side of the server alley. But I was just standing there by the Diet Coke dispenser, holding this little metal key, and I just started repeating table numbers. Out loud. Just standing there going, "Table 42, table 12, table 42, table 12." Over and over. And I wasn't closing the checks. I was just holding the key and saying the numbers. My manager, Dave, he had to physically come over and touch my arm and say my name a few times to get me to stop. And it's like, I know I'm doing it, I know I'm doing things completely out of order and making these repetitive motions or saying the same things, but I just get locked into it. It's not just tapping or folding, it's like my whole sequence of actions gets scrambled and then gets stuck on a loop. And it's terrifying because I have tables waiting, people want their change, and I'm just standing by the ice machine chanting numbers.
When you’re stuck doing the repetitive movement or phrase, can you stop it if someone tells you to?

Well, that's the thing, it's... it's not like a light switch. I wish it was. I wish someone could just yell "stop" and I'd snap out of it instantly, but it doesn't really work like that. Like I said about my manager, Dave, when I was doing the table numbers thing? He had to come over and physically touch my arm. And even then, it wasn't like, *boom*, I'm back. It's more like... like waking up from a really deep sleep where you're still groggy and confused for a second. He was saying my name, "Sarah, Sarah," and I heard him, but it felt like he was talking to me from underwater at first. And then I felt his hand on my arm, and that physical contact kind of pulled me back. But if someone just shouts at me from across the room? Like, if a customer was like, "Hey, waitress, stop doing that!" I don't know if that would work. It really seems to take someone getting right in my space, breaking that loop physically or repeating my name a few times until it finally registers. And it's so embarrassing because once I do stop, I have to look at them, and I know they've been watching me do this weird thing, and I have to pretend like everything is fine when my heart is just pounding out of my chest. So, yeah, I can stop, eventually, but it takes a lot of effort from whoever is trying to help me, and it's never just a simple "hey, cut it out" kind of thing. It's a whole process to get me un-stuck.
Between these episodes, have you noticed any changes in your memory, attention, or ability to think clearly in everyday life?

Well, no, not really. I mean, between those weird stuck moments, my brain feels totally normal. Actually, my memory is probably my best asset, which you kind of have to have in the service industry, right? I've been waitressing for a long time, and I can take a six-top's order without even writing it down half the time. I know exactly who gets the ranch dressing on the side, who has the weird gluten sensitivity but then orders a beer anyway, who wants their steak medium-rare but leaning towards rare... all of that. I keep it all straight in my head. 

So my attention is definitely there. If I couldn't think clearly, I wouldn't survive a Friday night dinner rush, let alone a Sunday brunch, which is honestly just organized chaos. It's really just those specific moments where I derail and get stuck. But once I'm out of it, or before it happens, I'm completely sharp. I still read a lot, and I've been taking a couple of community college classes here and there when I can afford the tuition, and I'm doing completely fine in those. I remember the lectures, I remember what I read in the textbooks. I remember where I put my keys, I remember to pay my rent on the first... well, usually, unless the payment portal is down, which happens way more than you'd think with my landlord's awful website, but that's a whole other story. 

But as far as my actual brain goes, like my everyday thinking and memory? It feels completely intact. I don't feel foggy or forgetful or confused at all. In fact, I'm almost hyper-aware of everything right now because I'm so anxious about when the next weird loop is going to happen, you know? I'm constantly scanning the restaurant, keeping track of my tables, watching my manager out of the corner of my eye to make sure he's not hovering. So I'd say my attention is almost too good sometimes, just because I'm on high alert. But no, no actual changes in how I think or remember things. It's just the freezing up that's the problem.
Have you noticed any rhythmic rocking, body swaying, or hand-flapping when these episodes happen?

Rocking or hand-flapping? No, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that, and nobody has mentioned me doing that either. It's actually kind of the exact opposite, which is what I was trying to explain earlier about that whole situation at work. 

Like, that time I was standing by the soda station? I wasn't swaying or moving my hands around at all. That’s exactly what scared everyone so much, and what terrified me—the fact that I just started freezing up right in the middle of service. It’s not extra movement, it’s more like my body just stops working right, and I start doing things completely out of order. Like I was saying, I had that cash drawer key in my hand, and I was supposed to be closing checks at the terminal, but instead I was just planted there by the Diet Coke dispenser, totally rigid, just repeating those table numbers over and over. 

You'd think if someone's brain is glitching, they'd be pacing or thrashing or, like you said, rocking back and forth, but I just become this weird statue. It's like my physical body just powers down, but my mouth keeps going with the wrong information. If I had been flapping my hands, maybe my manager would have noticed sooner, or maybe it would have just looked like I was having a panic attack or something, I don't know. But the freezing... it’s like I turn into a broken robot that’s just stuck on a loop. So, yeah, no rocking or swaying. It’s just that sudden freezing completely still, in the completely wrong place, holding a key and doing the completely wrong part of my job.
Before these recent work problems started, have you had similar repetitive movements or repetitive speech since childhood?

Since childhood? No, no, definitely not. This is... this is completely new. I mean, I was a pretty normal kid, you know? I did ballet for a few years, I played soccer in middle school—I was terrible at it, mostly just ran away from the ball, but I was out there running around like everyone else. I never got stuck or repeated things. If I had been doing this kind of stuff back then, my mom definitely would have had me in to see every specialist in the state. She was one of those moms who worried about every little sniffle or scraped knee. 

So, no, this whole thing, it really just started recently. And that's why it's so terrifying. I mean, I'm thirty-two years old, I've been working in restaurants since I was nineteen, and I've always been the one who could handle the pressure. I thrive in the weeds, you know? But then... then this started happening. Like I was saying before, it's just so bizarre. What really freaked everyone out at the restaurant—and what freaked *me* out—is that I just started freezing up right in the middle of a busy service. Or, like, doing things completely out of order. 

I know I mentioned this, but it’s just the perfect example... that time I was standing by the soda station? I was supposed to be at the POS terminal closing out checks. I had the cash drawer key right there in my hand. But instead of walking to the computer, I just walked over to the Diet Coke dispenser and stood there. Like a statue. Just holding the key and repeating table numbers out loud. "Table four, table twelve, table four, table twelve." Over and over. And it wasn't like I was doing it on purpose, or like it was a game. My body just... went to the wrong place and did the wrong thing, and then stopped working. I should have been closing checks, but I was just planted there by the sodas. It's so embarrassing to think about, Dave just staring at me while I'm holding a key and talking to the ice machine. So, yeah, nothing like this ever happened when I was a kid. It’s all brand new, and it’s completely ruining my ability to do my job. I mean, how can you be a waitress if you just randomly stop walking and start talking to the beverage station? You can't. You just can't.
Do you have any urges or sensations right before the episodes happen, like a buildup or pressure that goes away when you do the movement or say the phrase?

An urge? Like a... like I *need* to do it? No, God, no. There’s absolutely no buildup or pressure or anything like that. It’s not like... you know how when you feel a sneeze coming on, or when you’re about to cry and you get that tight feeling in your throat and you know it's happening? There’s nothing like that. Zero warning. 

One second I’m totally fine, just walking through the dining room thinking about getting more sourdough bread for table seven, and the next second, I’m just... stuck. And it definitely doesn’t feel like a relief when I start saying the words. You asked if the pressure goes away when I say the phrase? It’s really the exact opposite. Saying those table numbers over and over by the Diet Coke dispenser didn't relieve anything, it just... it’s like I was trapped inside my own mouth while it was happening. 

If I had some kind of warning, like a physical sensation or a tingling or literally anything, at least I could excuse myself, right? I could run to the back, maybe hide in the walk-in cooler behind the kegs until it passes. I mean, everyone in the service industry goes to the walk-in to have a moment when they're overwhelmed, that's just standard practice. You go in, you take a deep breath, you come back out. But I can't even do that because I never know it's about to happen. I don't get a five-second warning to get off the floor. I'm just doing my job, walking to the terminal, and then BAM, my brain just hijacks me. So no, no urges or pressure at all. It's basically just an ambush.
When one of these episodes starts, can you hold it back for a little while if you really try?

Hold it back? No, not at all. I mean, I really wish I could. If I could just, you know, white-knuckle my way through it and delay it for even five minutes, I absolutely would. In a restaurant, you have to hold back a lot of things—you hold back snapping at a rude customer, you hold back crying when you drop a tray of water glasses, you hold back needing to go to the bathroom for hours. You learn to suppress things until you're off the floor. But this? There is zero suppressing it. 

I know I keep sounding like a broken record bringing up that same exact story, but it’s just because it perfectly shows how little control I have over the whole thing. If I could hold it back, I wouldn't have just frozen up right in the middle of a busy service, you know? That’s exactly what scared everyone at work so badly. I was supposed to be doing my job, but instead, I was doing things completely out of order. If I had any ability to stop it or push it down, I would have walked to the computer to close those checks like I was supposed to. I wouldn't have just stood there by the soda station holding the cash drawer key like an idiot, repeating those table numbers over and over. 

I mean, somewhere deep in my brain, I knew I needed to move. I knew my manager was looking at me, I knew I had a table waiting for their change, but my body just wouldn't listen. It's not like holding your breath or fighting off a yawn where you have a say in the matter. It just takes over. I'm just stuck there freezing up, totally out of order. And it's so frustrating because I've always prided myself on being in control. When you're serving, you're the conductor of your section, right? You dictate the pace, you manage the flow. But with this... I have no say whatsoever. It just hijacks me, and I can't pause it or delay it or hold it back for even a single second.
Before these episodes happen, do you feel any uncomfortable urge or sensation that builds up and gets relieved by doing the movement or saying the phrase?

I... wait, didn't you just ask me that? I feel like we just went over this a minute ago. But no, really, the answer is still no. There is absolutely no uncomfortable urge, no physical sensation, no building up of pressure that gets relieved when I do it. Nothing like that at all. 

I know I'm repeating myself here too, but I really need you to understand this part, because that complete lack of warning is exactly what scared everyone at work so badly. If there was a buildup, maybe I could manage it, you know? I could step off the floor. But instead, I just started freezing up right in the middle of a busy service, completely out of nowhere. I started doing things completely out of order. Like I was telling you before with that whole incident—instead of closing out my checks at the computer like I was supposed to, I was just suddenly standing by the soda station holding the cash drawer key and repeating table numbers. 

There was no urge that made me walk over there, and there was definitely no relief when I started saying the numbers. It just happens. Boom. You're hijacked. No urge, no relief. Just me, stuck there, out of order, not doing the things I'm supposed to be doing. And honestly, it’s just exhausting trying to explain how sudden it is to people, because everyone thinks you must feel *something* coming on, like a migraine aura or a sneeze, but I promise you, doctor, there is nothing. One second I'm a waitress doing my job, and the next second I'm a statue by the Diet Coke dispenser. So no, no sensations or urges beforehand.
Do the movements or repeated phrases ever happen as brief, sudden jerks or vocal sounds that you can't control?

Brief, sudden jerks? Or like... vocal sounds? No, no, it's really not like that. It's not a twitch or a spasm or like... you know when you're falling asleep and your leg just kicks out of nowhere? It's not like that at all. And the sounds aren't just random noises or grunts or anything. 

Like I said, it's whole phrases. Whole strings of words. Like the table numbers I was telling you about. "Table four, table seven, table nine." Over and over. It's not a jerk, it's... it's a whole posture. I just freeze. I get completely stuck in one position, like holding that cash drawer key by the soda machine. I wasn't twitching or jerking around, I was just... frozen solid. 

I mean, if I was just having muscle spasms or making sudden noises, I feel like my manager would have thought I was having a seizure or Tourette's or something, right? But this was different. It's like my whole body just hits a pause button, but my mouth keeps going on a loop. It's so strange, because I'm fully aware that I'm standing there completely still, and I'm fully aware that I'm saying these things, but I can't break out of it. It's not a quick jerk that's over in a second. It's this whole... episode where I'm just stuck. So no, no sudden jerks or little vocal sounds. It's much more involved than that.
Before one of these episodes starts, do you get a brief urge or feeling that builds up and then goes away when you do the movement or say the phrase?

I... wait, I'm sorry, doctor, but didn't you just ask me that exact same thing? I feel like we just talked about this, like, two minutes ago. Are you... are you testing my memory or something? Because I promise you, my answer hasn't changed since the last time you asked. 

There is no urge. There is no feeling that builds up. There's no pressure cooker feeling that I have to release by doing it. Nothing. Zero. And honestly, it's starting to frustrate me a little bit that you keep asking, because I feel like I'm not explaining myself well enough if you have to keep checking. 

I really need you to understand that the total lack of warning, the fact that there's no buildup or urge, is the whole problem. That is exactly what scared everyone at work so badly. If I had an urge, I would have walked off the floor. I would have gone to the breakroom or the bathroom. But I didn't. I just started freezing up right in the middle of service, right when we were getting slammed. I started doing things completely out of order, totally out of nowhere. 

I know I keep bringing up that one shift, but it's just the best example. I was supposed to be walking to the POS system to close out my checks. That was the plan. But instead, with no warning, no urge, no feeling building up, I was just suddenly standing by the soda station. I was holding the cash drawer key—which I didn't even need at that moment—and I was just repeating table numbers over and over. "Table four, table seven, table nine." Just stuck there. 

There was no urge that made me do it, and saying the numbers didn't relieve anything. It's not like scratching an itch. It's just... a glitch. A total system failure where I'm suddenly doing everything wrong and I can't stop. So no, I don't get an urge. Not a brief one, not a long one. It just happens, and it's terrifying because I have absolutely zero warning before I'm just standing there looking crazy in front of my manager and half the restaurant.
Just before an episode starts, do you feel a strong urge or a buildup of tension that gets relieved when you do the movement or say the phrase?

Doctor... I... wait. Okay, I really don't mean to be rude, but are you writing any of this down? Because this is literally the exact same question you just asked me, and the time before that. I feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit here, sitting in this chair, just repeating myself on a loop. It's like you're trying to catch me in a lie or something, or maybe you're just not hearing what I'm saying? 

I'm going to say it one more time, and I really, really need you to hear me, okay? No. No urge. No tension. No relief. Absolutely zero buildup. 

I don't know how else to explain it to you. If there was tension, if there was some kind of warning sign, I wouldn't have been in the middle of the dining room when it happened. That's the whole reason everyone at the restaurant freaked out! Because it was so sudden. We were in the middle of the dinner rush, tickets printing non-stop, and I just... I froze. I started doing everything completely wrong, completely out of order. 

I was supposed to be at the computer. I had checks in my apron that needed to be closed out. But instead of walking to the POS, I just sort of... ended up by the soda station. And I was just standing there, like a statue, holding the key to the cash drawer. Why did I have the key? I don't know! I didn't need it. But I was holding it, and I was just staring at the Diet Coke dispenser, and I was saying, "Table four, table seven, table nine." Over and over. 

There was no tension that made me walk over there. I didn't feel a strong urge to hold the key. Saying the numbers didn't make me feel better or relieve any kind of pressure. I was just... stuck. It's like my brain just short-circuited and I was suddenly acting out a completely different script that made no sense. And I couldn't stop it, and I couldn't snap out of it, and I had absolutely no warning that it was going to happen. 

So please, doctor, I'm begging you, understand that it just happens. No urges. No tension. Just me, suddenly standing by the soda machine, completely out of order, scaring the hell out of my manager and my tables. Okay? Does that make sense now?
Just before one of these episodes starts, do you feel an urge that you can’t resist?

Okay, is this a joke? Seriously, doctor, is there a hidden camera in this office or something? Because you just asked me that. You literally just asked me if there's an urge, and the time before that, and the time before that! I just told you, like, thirty seconds ago, that there is absolutely no urge. 

I'm trying to be cooperative, I really am, because I came here for help, but I feel like you're just not listening to a single word coming out of my mouth. I don't know if this is some kind of psychiatric test where you try to make the patient mad to see how they react, or if you're just reading off a clipboard and ignoring my answers, but it's really upsetting me. I don't have an urge! I can't resist an urge that doesn't exist! 

I'm going to explain this one more time, okay? I'm going to lay it out with as much detail as I possibly can so we can please, please move on. What scared everyone at work—my manager, the other servers, the kitchen staff—is that I started freezing up in the middle of service, or just doing things completely out of order. I've been doing this job a long time, I know how the flow of a dinner rush works, but suddenly my brain just... derailed. 

Instead of closing checks like I was supposed to be doing, I was just standing by the soda station holding the cash drawer key and repeating table numbers. I had no reason to have that key! I wasn't at the register! But there I was, just glued to the floor by the Diet Coke, chanting "Table four, table seven, table nine" while my tables were waiting for their change. 

There was no little tickle in my brain telling me to walk over there. There was no irresistible urge that I was trying to fight off. It just happened. I was just suddenly doing everything out of order and freezing up. I really, really don't know how to make that any clearer for you. Do you have that written down now? No urge. Just freezing up. Please tell me you got it this time.
Did you have any tics—like blinking, grimacing, shoulder shrugging, or throat clearing—when you were a child?

Oh, okay, a different question. Thank you. Um... no. No, I didn't have anything like that. 

I mean, I guess I bit my nails a little bit in elementary school if I was nervous about a spelling test or something, but that's just normal kid stuff, right? Not... not what you're talking about. I never had any weird blinking things, or making faces, or shrugging my shoulders over and over. I was actually a really calm, still kid. I took some ballet classes when I was like, eight or nine, and I was always very focused on my posture and exactly how I moved. My mom used to say I was almost too serious about it for my age. So I never had any twitches or throat clearing or anything that I couldn't control. 

And honestly, doctor, that's part of why this whole situation right now is so completely terrifying to me, and to my family, and to everyone who knows me. Because I've never had anything even close to this happen before. Growing up, through high school, even when I was taking some classes at the community college a few years back, my body always did exactly what I told it to do. I was always in the driver's seat. I never had these... these glitches where I just freeze up out of nowhere. 

So, no, looking back, there was absolutely nothing like that when I was a child. I was completely normal.
Just before an episode starts, do you ever feel an irresistible urge that gets relieved when you do the movement or say the phrase?

Doctor, are you... I'm sorry, I'm just trying to understand. Did you lose your place on your notepad? Because we literally just went over this, twice, right before you asked me about being a kid. I really, really don't know why you keep asking me about an urge. It's making me feel like you're not listening to a single word I'm saying, and it's honestly making my heart pound because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here. 

I will say it again, as clearly and with as much detail as I possibly can, because I really need you to write this down so we can move on. There is no urge. There is no relief. What scared everyone at work so badly—and I mean really scared them, my manager was practically in tears—is the fact that there's no warning at all. I just start freezing up right in the middle of service, or I start doing things completely out of order. 

Like, I'll be right in the middle of a massive dinner rush, tickets are flying, the kitchen is yelling, and instead of closing checks like I'm supposed to be doing, my brain just... stops working right. I end up standing all the way over by the soda station, just totally frozen. And I'm holding the cash drawer key for absolutely no reason, just standing there like a mannequin, repeating table numbers out loud. I don't feel an urge to hold the key! I don't feel a buildup of tension that makes me want to stand by the soda machine! It just happens, and I'm stuck there doing things in the completely wrong order while my tables are waiting for me. 

Please, please tell me you understand this time. No urges. Just freezing up and doing things out of order. Can we please talk about something else now?

doctor.intent: Open the interview and identify the main presenting complaint so I can narrow the diagnostic possibilities.
doctor.question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: What scared everyone at work is that I started freezing up in the middle of service or doing things out of order, like standing by the soda station holding the cash drawer key and repeating table numbers instead of closing checks.
target_item.reason: This is the first turn of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S022.

patient.answer: Well, hi, Doctor. I'm... I'm here because my manager at the restaurant told me I had to come see someone if I wanted to keep my shifts. I've been a waitress there for three years, you know? And I'm usually really good, like, I can balance four plates on one arm and I never forget a side of ranch. But lately, things have just been... getting tangled up. What really scared everyone at work, and I guess what scared me too, is that I started just... freezing up in the middle of service. Like, right in the middle of the dinner rush. Or I'd start doing things completely out of order. The other night, I was just standing by the soda station for I don't even know how long, holding the key to the cash drawer, and I was just repeating table numbers out loud. "Table four, table twelve, table nine." Over and over. I was supposed to be closing out checks, but I just stood there with the key, staring at the ice machine, saying the numbers. My manager had to come tap me on the shoulder and ask me what I was doing, and I couldn't even really explain it to him because it felt like the numbers were the only thing that made sense right then. So he told me I couldn't come back until I got a doctor's note saying I was okay to work.

inference.note: New presentation suggests a dissociative/functional episode with altered behavior and possible stupor, while also keeping an organic mental disorder and borderline personality disorder in the differential; no single diagnosis is yet confirmed.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a fixed memory gap for the period of impaired behavior, which would support a dissociative amnesia/functional dissociation over other causes.

patient.answer: No, I don't think so. I mean, it's not like a blackout or anything like that. I remember standing there. I remember the cold air coming off the ice machine, and I remember the exact feeling of the metal key pressing into the palm of my hand. It had a little jagged edge on one side that I kept running my thumb over. And I remember hearing myself say the numbers. "Table four, table twelve, table nine." It wasn't like I was asleep or unconscious. I was completely awake. But it's more like... my brain just gets stuck on a loop, you know? Like a record skipping, if people even know what that means anymore. I used to have this old record player in my dorm room when I was taking classes at the community college—just a few semesters, business admin, though I never finished—and it would hit a scratch and just play the same three seconds of a song over and over until you physically moved the needle. That's what it feels like. I'm there, I'm aware of my surroundings, I can see the wait station and hear the kitchen printer going off, but I just can't move the needle myself. I just have to keep doing the thing I'm doing until someone else, like my manager, comes along and kind of bumps the record player for me. So, no, the memory is all there, it's just... the control isn't, I guess? Or the ability to do the next step just vanishes.

doctor.intent: To assess whether the episodes are sudden stress-related dissociative episodes rather than a chronic personality pattern or neurologic/other cognitive issue
doctor.question: Do these episodes usually happen when you’re under a lot of stress?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the episodes of disorganized behavior (freezing up, repeating numbers) are triggered by stress, which is not explicitly covered in the symptom profile.

patient.answer: I mean... I don't really know if stress is the trigger. You'd think so, right? Because a dinner rush is stressful. It's loud, the kitchen gets backed up, people are waving you down for refills, and the ticket machine is just printing and printing. But the thing is, I've worked in restaurants since I was nineteen. I actually used to thrive on that energy. I used to love the chaos of a Friday night when every table is full and you're just flying through the dining room. It felt like a dance. So the stress... it's not new stress, you know? And it doesn't only happen when it's crazy busy. Like, last Tuesday, it was a totally dead afternoon shift. Maybe three tables in the whole place. I was rolling silverware in the back, which is usually the most relaxing part of the day, just folding the napkins, tucking in the forks and knives, making these neat little bundles. It's so repetitive and quiet. And I was just standing there, and suddenly I couldn't stop folding this one napkin. I just kept smoothing it out, folding it in half, unfolding it, smoothing it out again. Over and over. There was no rush, no one yelling for me, no stress at all. Just me and this black cloth napkin. I must have stood there doing it for twenty minutes before the bartender walked back and asked if I was okay. So... I guess I'm not really sure if stress has anything to do with it, because it seems to happen whether I'm carrying a tray of hot food through a crowd or just standing in an empty room doing side work. It's just so unpredictable, which honestly is what stresses me out the most now. The not knowing when the record is going to skip again.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the episodes are involuntary/automatic or intentionally produced, which helps distinguish dissociative/functional symptoms from personality-related or organic causes.
doctor.question: During these episodes, do you ever feel like you are choosing or acting them out on purpose?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient feels like they are intentionally choosing or acting out the abnormal behaviors on purpose (assessing for factitious disorder or malingering). This specific question about the intentionality of the behavior is not covered by any of the symptom profiles.

patient.answer: No, no, definitely not on purpose. I mean, why would I? It's embarrassing. It's so embarrassing. Like with the napkin thing I just mentioned, folding and unfolding it... if I was doing that on purpose, I would have stopped the second I realized how ridiculous it looked. But I couldn't. It's like... it's like my hands were doing it, and my brain was watching my hands do it, but there was no connection between the two. There's no part of me that thinks, "Oh, I'm going to stand by the soda machine and say table numbers now." I don't want to do these things. I want to be working. I need my job. I have rent, I have my car payment—it's a 2014 Civic, and it's mostly reliable, but it needs new brake pads soon, and I can't afford that if I'm not picking up shifts. So, no, I'm not choosing this. It feels like the opposite of choosing. It feels like the choice is completely taken away from me. I'm just sort of trapped inside the action while it's happening, waiting for it to be over, waiting for someone to snap me out of it so I can just go back to being normal and doing my job. I'd give anything to just be able to choose to stop when it happens.

doctor.intent: To determine whether there is evidence of a neurological or medical cause for the episodes, which would support an organic dissociative/fugue-like condition rather than a primary personality disorder.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of seizures, which is a medical condition not covered by any of the provided psychiatric symptom profiles (Delusions, Hallucinations, Disorganized Abnormal Behavior, Negative Symptoms, Functional Impairment, Duration, Psychotic Symptoms Duration).

patient.answer: A seizure? Like, falling down and shaking? No, I've never had anything like that. I mean, my aunt on my mom's side had epilepsy, I think? Or maybe it was my great-aunt. I remember my mom talking about it when I was really little, how they had to be careful with flashing lights and stuff. But I've never had anything like that happen to me. I've never passed out or convulsed or bitten my tongue. And like I was saying before, I'm completely awake when these weird stuck moments happen. My eyes are open, I'm standing up, I'm not falling over or losing my balance. I'm just... frozen in whatever I'm doing. So it doesn't feel like a medical emergency in that way, you know? It's not like my body is spasming. It's just my actions that get stuck. I've never even fainted in my life, honestly. Not even when I had to get my blood drawn for a physical a few years ago, and I hate needles. I get super lightheaded, but I always stay conscious. So, no, definitely no seizures. Unless... I mean, unless there's a type of seizure where you just stand there and repeat things? But even then, I feel like a doctor would have caught that when I was younger. I was a pretty healthy kid, mostly just ear infections and stuff. So, yeah, no seizures that I know of.

patient.answer: Well, yes, I mean, like I was saying with the napkin, right? Folding and unfolding it. That's definitely one of them. But it's not just the folding. It's... it's the whole pattern of how I get stuck, and it's really starting to freak people out at work. What really scared everyone, and honestly scared me too, is that I started freezing up right in the middle of service. Like, right in the thick of it. I'll be in the middle of doing something completely normal, and then I just... derail. Like, the other day, I was supposed to be closing out checks. We have this old point-of-sale system, it's super clunky, you have to use a physical key to pop the cash drawer if you're settling a cash payment. So I had the cash drawer key in my hand, and I was standing by the soda station, which isn't even where the terminal is. The terminal is on the other side of the server alley. But I was just standing there by the Diet Coke dispenser, holding this little metal key, and I just started repeating table numbers. Out loud. Just standing there going, "Table 42, table 12, table 42, table 12." Over and over. And I wasn't closing the checks. I was just holding the key and saying the numbers. My manager, Dave, he had to physically come over and touch my arm and say my name a few times to get me to stop. And it's like, I know I'm doing it, I know I'm doing things completely out of order and making these repetitive motions or saying the same things, but I just get locked into it. It's not just tapping or folding, it's like my whole sequence of actions gets scrambled and then gets stuck on a loop. And it's terrifying because I have tables waiting, people want their change, and I'm just standing by the ice machine chanting numbers.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the repetitive behaviors are intentional/goal-directed stereotyped movements versus involuntary neurologic or dissociative phenomena.

patient.answer: Well, that's the thing, it's... it's not like a light switch. I wish it was. I wish someone could just yell "stop" and I'd snap out of it instantly, but it doesn't really work like that. Like I said about my manager, Dave, when I was doing the table numbers thing? He had to come over and physically touch my arm. And even then, it wasn't like, *boom*, I'm back. It's more like... like waking up from a really deep sleep where you're still groggy and confused for a second. He was saying my name, "Sarah, Sarah," and I heard him, but it felt like he was talking to me from underwater at first. And then I felt his hand on my arm, and that physical contact kind of pulled me back. But if someone just shouts at me from across the room? Like, if a customer was like, "Hey, waitress, stop doing that!" I don't know if that would work. It really seems to take someone getting right in my space, breaking that loop physically or repeating my name a few times until it finally registers. And it's so embarrassing because once I do stop, I have to look at them, and I know they've been watching me do this weird thing, and I have to pretend like everything is fine when my heart is just pounding out of my chest. So, yeah, I can stop, eventually, but it takes a lot of effort from whoever is trying to help me, and it's never just a simple "hey, cut it out" kind of thing. It's a whole process to get me un-stuck.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the episodes are primarily abnormal movements/behavior without altered consciousness, which would support an organic cognitive disorder over catatonia or conversion disorder.
doctor.question: Between these episodes, have you noticed any changes in your memory, attention, or ability to think clearly in everyday life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about cognitive symptoms such as changes in memory, attention, or clear thinking, which are not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I mean, between those weird stuck moments, my brain feels totally normal. Actually, my memory is probably my best asset, which you kind of have to have in the service industry, right? I've been waitressing for a long time, and I can take a six-top's order without even writing it down half the time. I know exactly who gets the ranch dressing on the side, who has the weird gluten sensitivity but then orders a beer anyway, who wants their steak medium-rare but leaning towards rare... all of that. I keep it all straight in my head. 

So my attention is definitely there. If I couldn't think clearly, I wouldn't survive a Friday night dinner rush, let alone a Sunday brunch, which is honestly just organized chaos. It's really just those specific moments where I derail and get stuck. But once I'm out of it, or before it happens, I'm completely sharp. I still read a lot, and I've been taking a couple of community college classes here and there when I can afford the tuition, and I'm doing completely fine in those. I remember the lectures, I remember what I read in the textbooks. I remember where I put my keys, I remember to pay my rent on the first... well, usually, unless the payment portal is down, which happens way more than you'd think with my landlord's awful website, but that's a whole other story. 

But as far as my actual brain goes, like my everyday thinking and memory? It feels completely intact. I don't feel foggy or forgetful or confused at all. In fact, I'm almost hyper-aware of everything right now because I'm so anxious about when the next weird loop is going to happen, you know? I'm constantly scanning the restaurant, keeping track of my tables, watching my manager out of the corner of my eye to make sure he's not hovering. So I'd say my attention is almost too good sometimes, just because I'm on high alert. But no, no actual changes in how I think or remember things. It's just the freezing up that's the problem.

patient.answer:
Rocking or hand-flapping? No, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that, and nobody has mentioned me doing that either. It's actually kind of the exact opposite, which is what I was trying to explain earlier about that whole situation at work. 

Like, that time I was standing by the soda station? I wasn't swaying or moving my hands around at all. That’s exactly what scared everyone so much, and what terrified me—the fact that I just started freezing up right in the middle of service. It’s not extra movement, it’s more like my body just stops working right, and I start doing things completely out of order. Like I was saying, I had that cash drawer key in my hand, and I was supposed to be closing checks at the terminal, but instead I was just planted there by the Diet Coke dispenser, totally rigid, just repeating those table numbers over and over. 

You'd think if someone's brain is glitching, they'd be pacing or thrashing or, like you said, rocking back and forth, but I just become this weird statue. It's like my physical body just powers down, but my mouth keeps going with the wrong information. If I had been flapping my hands, maybe my manager would have noticed sooner, or maybe it would have just looked like I was having a panic attack or something, I don't know. But the freezing... it’s like I turn into a broken robot that’s just stuck on a loop. So, yeah, no rocking or swaying. It’s just that sudden freezing completely still, in the completely wrong place, holding a key and doing the completely wrong part of my job.

doctor.intent: Differentiate catatonia from stereotypic movement disorder by assessing whether the repetitive behavior occurs across many situations as a longstanding pattern
doctor.question: Before these recent work problems started, have you had similar repetitive movements or repetitive speech since childhood?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the onset of the repetitive movements and speech to determine if this disorganized/abnormal behavior has been present since childhood or is a recent development.

patient.answer:
Since childhood? No, no, definitely not. This is... this is completely new. I mean, I was a pretty normal kid, you know? I did ballet for a few years, I played soccer in middle school—I was terrible at it, mostly just ran away from the ball, but I was out there running around like everyone else. I never got stuck or repeated things. If I had been doing this kind of stuff back then, my mom definitely would have had me in to see every specialist in the state. She was one of those moms who worried about every little sniffle or scraped knee. 

So, no, this whole thing, it really just started recently. And that's why it's so terrifying. I mean, I'm thirty-two years old, I've been working in restaurants since I was nineteen, and I've always been the one who could handle the pressure. I thrive in the weeds, you know? But then... then this started happening. Like I was saying before, it's just so bizarre. What really freaked everyone out at the restaurant—and what freaked *me* out—is that I just started freezing up right in the middle of a busy service. Or, like, doing things completely out of order. 

I know I mentioned this, but it’s just the perfect example... that time I was standing by the soda station? I was supposed to be at the POS terminal closing out checks. I had the cash drawer key right there in my hand. But instead of walking to the computer, I just walked over to the Diet Coke dispenser and stood there. Like a statue. Just holding the key and repeating table numbers out loud. "Table four, table twelve, table four, table twelve." Over and over. And it wasn't like I was doing it on purpose, or like it was a game. My body just... went to the wrong place and did the wrong thing, and then stopped working. I should have been closing checks, but I was just planted there by the sodas. It's so embarrassing to think about, Dave just staring at me while I'm holding a key and talking to the ice machine. So, yeah, nothing like this ever happened when I was a kid. It’s all brand new, and it’s completely ruining my ability to do my job. I mean, how can you be a waitress if you just randomly stop walking and start talking to the beverage station? You can't. You just can't.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the episodes are involuntary motor or vocal tics that worsen with stress and can be briefly suppressed, versus a functional/psychogenic pattern.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about premonitory urges or sensations, which are characteristic of tics. The patient's symptom profile does not include tics or any such urges before her episodes of disorganized behavior.

patient.answer:
An urge? Like a... like I *need* to do it? No, God, no. There’s absolutely no buildup or pressure or anything like that. It’s not like... you know how when you feel a sneeze coming on, or when you’re about to cry and you get that tight feeling in your throat and you know it's happening? There’s nothing like that. Zero warning. 

One second I’m totally fine, just walking through the dining room thinking about getting more sourdough bread for table seven, and the next second, I’m just... stuck. And it definitely doesn’t feel like a relief when I start saying the words. You asked if the pressure goes away when I say the phrase? It’s really the exact opposite. Saying those table numbers over and over by the Diet Coke dispenser didn't relieve anything, it just... it’s like I was trapped inside my own mouth while it was happening. 

If I had some kind of warning, like a physical sensation or a tingling or literally anything, at least I could excuse myself, right? I could run to the back, maybe hide in the walk-in cooler behind the kegs until it passes. I mean, everyone in the service industry goes to the walk-in to have a moment when they're overwhelmed, that's just standard practice. You go in, you take a deep breath, you come back out. But I can't even do that because I never know it's about to happen. I don't get a five-second warning to get off the floor. I'm just doing my job, walking to the terminal, and then BAM, my brain just hijacks me. So no, no urges or pressure at all. It's basically just an ambush.

patient.answer:
Hold it back? No, not at all. I mean, I really wish I could. If I could just, you know, white-knuckle my way through it and delay it for even five minutes, I absolutely would. In a restaurant, you have to hold back a lot of things—you hold back snapping at a rude customer, you hold back crying when you drop a tray of water glasses, you hold back needing to go to the bathroom for hours. You learn to suppress things until you're off the floor. But this? There is zero suppressing it. 

I know I keep sounding like a broken record bringing up that same exact story, but it’s just because it perfectly shows how little control I have over the whole thing. If I could hold it back, I wouldn't have just frozen up right in the middle of a busy service, you know? That’s exactly what scared everyone at work so badly. I was supposed to be doing my job, but instead, I was doing things completely out of order. If I had any ability to stop it or push it down, I would have walked to the computer to close those checks like I was supposed to. I wouldn't have just stood there by the soda station holding the cash drawer key like an idiot, repeating those table numbers over and over. 

I mean, somewhere deep in my brain, I knew I needed to move. I knew my manager was looking at me, I knew I had a table waiting for their change, but my body just wouldn't listen. It's not like holding your breath or fighting off a yawn where you have a say in the matter. It just takes over. I'm just stuck there freezing up, totally out of order. And it's so frustrating because I've always prided myself on being in control. When you're serving, you're the conductor of your section, right? You dictate the pace, you manage the flow. But with this... I have no say whatsoever. It just hijacks me, and I can't pause it or delay it or hold it back for even a single second.
